etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English beten, from Old English bēatan (“to beat, pound, strike, lash, dash, thrust, hurt, injure”), from Proto-West Germanic *bautan, from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to push, strike”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewd- (“to hit, strike”).

Compare Old Irish fo·botha (“he threatened”), Latin confutō (“I strike down”), fūstis (“stick, club”), Albanian bahe (“sling”), Lithuanian baudžiù, Old Armenian բութ (butʻ)).

definitions.definition: A stroke; a blow.

quote.citation: 1687, [John Dryden], “(please specify the page number)”, in The Hind and the Panther. A Poem, in Three Parts, 2nd edition, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson […], →OCLC:
quote.text: He,  […] with a careless beat, / Struck out the mute creation at a heat.

definitions.definition: A pulsation or throb.
(music) A pulse on the beat level, the metric level at which pulses are heard as the basic unit. Thus a beat is the basic time unit of a piece.
(music) The rhythm signalled by a conductor or other musician to the members of a group of musicians.
A rhythm.
The instrumental portion of a piece of hip-hop music.
The interference between two tones of almost equal frequency
(authorship) A short pause in a play, screenplay, or teleplay, for dramatic or comedic effect.
The route patrolled by a police officer or a guard.

quote.citation: 1886, Arthur Conan Doyle, chapter 3, in A Study in Scarlet:
quote.text: There has been a bad business during the night at 3, Lauriston Gardens, off the Brixton Road. Our man on the beat saw a light there about two in the morning, and as the house was an empty one, suspected that something was amiss.

quote.citation: 2019 January 29, Mike Masnick, “How My High School Destroyed An Immigrant Kid's Life Because He Drew The School's Mascot”, in Techdirt‎[1]:
quote.text: […] the rise of embedding police into schools – so-called School Resource Officers (SROs), who are employed by the local police, but whose “beat” is a school. Those officers report to the local police department and not the school, and can, and frequently do, have different priorities.

definitions.definition: (journalism) The primary focus of a reporter's stories (such as police/courts, education, city government, business etc.).

quote.citation: 2020 April, Elizabeth Kolbert, “Why we won't avoid a climate catastrophe[2]”, in National Geographic:
quote.text: As an adult, I became a journalist whose beat is the environment. In a way, I’ve turned my youthful preoccupations into a profession.

definitions.definition: (by extension) An area of a person's responsibility, especially
(dated) An act of reporting news or scientific results before a rival; a scoop.

quote.citation: 1898, unknown author, Scribner's Magazine, volume 24:
quote.text: It's a beat on the whole country.

definitions.definition: (colloquial, dated) That which beats, or surpasses, another or others.
(dated or obsolete, Southern US) A precinct.
(Australia) An area frequented by gay men in search of sexual activity. See gay beat.
(dated) A place of habitual or frequent resort.
(archaic) A low cheat or swindler.

quote.citation: 1884 December 10, Mark Twain [pseudonym; Samuel Langhorne Clemens], chapter XXVIII, in The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn: (Tom Sawyer’s Comrade) […], London: Chatto & Windus, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: “If I get away I sha’n’t be here,” I says, “to prove these rapscallions ain’t your uncles, and I couldn’t do it if I was here. I could swear they was beats and bummers, that’s all, though that’s worth something.

definitions.definition: (hunting) The act of scouring, or ranging over, a tract of land to rouse or drive out game; also, those so engaged, collectively.

quote.citation: 1911, Hedley Peek, Frederick George Aflalo, Encyclopaedia of Sport:
quote.text: Bears coming out of holes in the rocks at the last moment, when the beat is close to them.

definitions.definition: (fencing) A smart tap on the adversary's blade.
(slang) A makeup look; compare beat one's face.

quote.citation: 2018, Leah Prinzivalli, “Kylie Jenner Shared a Sneak Peek of Her New Kylie Cosmetics Blush on Instagram”, in Allure‎[3]:
quote.text: She made sure to give fans all the details about her beat in the caption.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To hit; to strike.

quote.citation: 1825?, “Hannah Limbrick, Executed for Murder”, in The Newgate Calendar: comprising interesting memoirs of the most notorious characters, page 231:
quote.text: Thomas Limbrick, who was only nine years of age, said he lived with his mother when Deborah was beat: that his mother throwed her down all along with her hands; and then against a wall  […]

quote.citation: 1988, Emily Honig, Gail Hershatter, “Divorce”, in Personal Voices: Chinese Women in the 1980's‎[4], Stanford, Cali.: Stanford University Press, →ISBN, →LCCN, →OCLC, page 219:
quote.text: The case of a woman named Qu Hua from Qiqihaer, Heilongjiang, illustrates this possibility. She married a worker named Xu Baocheng in 1980, and they got along very well until she gave birth to a girl. Then Xu immediately began to beat Qu, and forced her and the baby to live in a small shack.

quote.citation: 2012 August 21, Ed Pilkington, “Death penalty on trial: should Reggie Clemons live or die?”, in The Guardian‎[5]:
quote.text: In this account of events, the cards were stacked against Clemons from the beginning. His appeal lawyers have argued that he was physically beaten into making a confession, the jury was wrongfully selected and misdirected, and his conviction largely achieved on individual testimony with no supporting forensic evidence presented.

quote.citation: 2021 March 10, Drachinifel, 5:50 from the start, in Guadalcanal Campaign - The Big Night Battle: Night 1 (IJN 3(?) : 2 USN)‎[6], archived from the original on 17 October 2022:
quote.text: The attack also afforded Helena to a front-seat view of literal air-to-air melee combat, as one Wildcat pilot of the Cactus Air Force, who was swooping in to help break up the attack, found himself out of machine-gun ammo; instead, he dropped his landing gear, positioned himself above the nearest bomber, and begun beating it to death, in midair, using his landing gear as clubs.  After a bit of evasive action that the fighter easily kept up with, the repeated slamming broke something important, and the bomber spiralled down into the sea.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To strike or pound repeatedly, usually in some sort of rhythm.
(intransitive) To strike repeatedly; to inflict repeated blows; to knock vigorously or loudly.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Judges 19:22:
quote.text: […]  the men of the city, certain sons of Belial, beset the house round about, and beat at the door  […]

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Jonah 4:8:
quote.text: The sun beat upon the head of Jonah, that he fainted, and wished in himself to die.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis Bacon, “Of Envy”, in Essayes:
quote.text: This public envy, seemeth to beat chiefly upon principal officers or ministers, rather than upon kings, and estates themselves.

quote.citation: 1662 January 1, John Dryden, To the Lord Chancellor Hyde, line 144:
quote.text: Sees rolling tempests vainly beat below.

quote.citation: 1850, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, “Twilight”, in The Seaside and the Fireside:
quote.text: What tale do the roaring ocean, / And the nightwind, bleak and wild, / As they beat at the crazy casement, / Tell to that little child?

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To move with pulsation or throbbing.

quote.citation: 1812–18, George Gordon Lord Byron, Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, canto 3, verse 21:
quote.text: A thousand hearts beat happily.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto IV:
quote.text: O heart, how fares it with thee now,⁠That thou should’st fail from thy desire,⁠Who scarcely darest to inquire,‘What is it makes me beat so low?’

definitions.definition: (transitive) To win against; to defeat or overcome; to do or be better than (someone); to excel in a particular, competitive event.

quote.citation: 1991, Richard Thompson (lyrics and music), “1952 Vincent Black Lightning”:
quote.text: There's nothing in this world beats a 52 Vincent and a red-headed girl.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, nautical) To sail to windward using a series of alternate tacks across the wind.
(transitive) To strike (water, foliage etc.) in order to drive out game; to travel through (a forest etc.) for hunting.

quote.citation: 1955, Robin Jenkins, The Cone-Gatherers, Canongate, published 2012, page 81:
quote.text: The part of the wood to be beaten for deer sloped all the way from the roadside to the loch.

definitions.definition: To mix food in a rapid fashion. Compare whip.
(transitive, UK, in haggling for a price of a buyer) To persuade the seller to reduce a price.
(transitive) To indicate by beating or drumming.
To tread, as a path.

quote.citation: 1712, Sir Richard Blackmore, Creation: A Philosophical Poem, book 1:
quote.text: While I this unexampled task essay, / Pass awful gulfs, and beat my painful way, / Celestial Dove! divine assistance bring, / Sustain me on thy strong-extended wing,

definitions.definition: To exercise severely; to perplex; to trouble.

quote.citation: 1693, John Locke, Some Thoughts Concerning Education:
quote.text: I know not why any one should waste his time, and beat his head about the Latin grammar, who does not intend to be a critick, or make speeches, and write dispatches in it.

definitions.definition: To be in agitation or doubt.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: to still my beating mind

definitions.definition: To make a sound when struck.
(military, intransitive) To make a succession of strokes on a drum.
To sound with more or less rapid alternations of greater and lesser intensity, so as to produce a pulsating effect; said of instruments, tones, or vibrations not perfectly in unison.
(transitive) To arrive at a place before someone.
(intransitive, MLE, MTE, slang, vulgar) To have sexual intercourse.

quote.citation: 2017-02-08, “Big (Millie B reply)”‎[7]performed by Sophie Aspin:
quote.text: Millie B gets ten shags a week. New day, different guy, that's just peek. You can't name a guy that you haven't tried to beat. You can't name a guy that you haven't tried to beat.

definitions.definition: (transitive, slang) To rob; to cheat or scam.

quote.citation: 1900, Fame, quoting Retail Trade Advocate, page 472:
quote.text: When one of 'em runs up a bill here, then goes off and deals somewhere else, and dodges me every time he sees me, that's the man I'm after with a sharp stick. [...] Honest people often get into tight places, and we would rather help 'em than hurt 'em then. But some just try to beat you.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bet (simple past of beten "to beat"), from Old English bēot (simple past of bēatan "to beat"). Middle English bet would regularly yield *beet; the modern form is influenced by the present stem and the past participle beaten. Pronunciations with /ɛ/ (from Middle English bette, alternative simple past of beten) are possibly analogous to read (/ɹɛd/), led, met, etc.

definitions.definition: simple past tense of beat
(especially colloquial) past participle of beat
(US slang) Exhausted.

quote.citation: 1957, Jack Kerouac, chapter 10, in On the Road, Viking Press, →OCLC, part 2:
quote.text: I stayed in San Francisco a week and had the beatest time of my life. Marylou and I walked around for miles, looking for food-money.

definitions.definition: (slang) Dilapidated, beat up.
(African-American Vernacular and gay slang) Having impressively attractive makeup.
(slang) Boring.
(slang, of a person) Ugly.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From beatnik, or beat generation.

definitions.definition: A beatnik.

quote.citation: 2008 March, David Wills, Beatdom, number 3:
quote.text: The beats were pioneers with no destination, changing the world one impulse at a time.

definitions.definition: Relating to the Beat Generation.
